greeting.text: Pyke sits on the granary steps, the chain coiled beside him. "Forty-one people," he says. "I counted. I count things." He turns the plumb-bob in his fingers. "Nobody's sent word from downriver. I keep expecting a letter, but there isn't one. I've worked out why: there's nothing to say. I stopped being paid. That's the whole punishment."

"Started again," Pyke says, drawing the chain straight along the lane. "Whole valley. From the ford." He doesn't look upset. He's got three years of guaranteed work. "Somebody down there lost a lot of paper. I feel for whoever's answering for it, but I won't pretend I'm sorry about the rest."

choices.label: Do they know who did it?

greeting.text: Pyke gives you a look as if you've moved up a floor. "Coyle's had word you're on the books," he says. "Not from me. It came with the wages." He winds the chain. "I'll tell you what I'd tell anybody: they pay on the day, and they've never short-changed me. Whatever else happens, they pay on the day."

choices.label: That's all it takes, is it.

greeting.text: Pyke spots what you're carrying before he sees your face. For a moment he says nothing. Then: "That's not a working copy. That's the fair one. It's got the totals in." He wipes his hands on his coat twice, something you've never seen him do. "I've dragged chain for about a third of that. I've never seen the sheet."

choices.label: Read it to me. All of it.
Nothing. I wanted somebody to see me holding it.

greeting.text: Pyke's chain is gone. The coil-hook on the granary wall is empty. He sits on the steps beside it, hands on his knees. "They've taken the work off me," he says, as flatly as if he were talking about the weather. "No reason given. There won't be one. A young man has come up from Greyhythe. He's got the ground, and my instrument with it." He looks at the hook. "I'm not blaming you. I've tried, and I can't make the blame stay put. But it took some work to get there, and I'd rather you knew that."

choices.label: I'll get it back for you.

greeting.text: Pyke sees you coming and slips the plumb-bob into his pocket, which he doesn't usually do. "You'll want to hear about the man," he says.

Pyke has the chain stretched along the lane, though he isn't measuring anything. "There's a line on my docket that isn't about my wages," he says. "Different hand from the counting house. It's a question: whether the chainman at Rivermark has been keeping company." He straightens slowly. "I've been paid on the day for three years. Nobody's wanted anything from me but chain. I haven't answered it. There's a space, and I've left it blank."
"So you went," Pyke says, quietly pleased. "How was he? He's always been decent to me. Asked after my knee. No reason he'd know about my knee."

choices.label: He answered everything I asked him.
How many marks have you painted for him, Pyke?
I've seen your mark in two places now.

greeting.text: "Corse," Pyke says when you give him the name. "Ludo Corse. That'll be him. Never met a man less worth the trouble of finding out about." He settles the chain over his shoulder. "He's been up twice in three years. Perfectly civil both times. Paid on the day."

choices.label: How many marks have you painted for him?

greeting.text: You set the note on the step beside him. Pyke reads it at arm's length and hands it back. "That's mine," he says. "Fourteen days at one and threepence. What about it?"

choices.label: There's no name on it. There's a mark.

greeting.text: "Still at it," Pyke says. "The counting house keeps every honoured note for a year before burning them. They're in the tray under the long desk. Mine'll be there with the rest. I don't know why you want it. It's a receipt."

"Wages," Pyke says when you ask again. He sighs and sits on the step. "Right. I'm paid at the counting house. The counting house isn't paying me; it's honouring a note for somebody who is. That's how everyone in town gets paid, unless they're paid in bread."

choices.label: Then I want to see the note.

greeting.text: "You put it back, then," Pyke says, neither pleased nor displeased. "Good. There's four hundred notes in that tray. Each one is somebody's fortnight, and none of them are anybody's business." He draws the chain straight. "Mine'll be burnt by spring with the rest."

choices.label: How many marks have you painted this year?

greeting.text: Pyke spots the bob in your hand and laughs, at ease with you. "Still collecting," he says. "How many's that now? Go on. I want to hear the number from somebody who isn't me."

Pyke has the chain half stretched along the lane, one end under his boot. "You're back," he says, mildly surprised. "Nobody comes back. They ask about the mark, I tell them what it is, and that's the last I see of them." He straightens. "So you've either thought of a better question or you're at a loose end."

Pyke has the chain half stretched along the lane, one end under his boot. "Come to watch a man drag a chain," he says. "It's the most interesting thing on this street. That's a poor look-out for the street."
A hundred feet of flat iron chain hangs over one of his shoulders. The plumb-bob turns slowly on its line, its brass face stamped with the mark: a bob hanging inside a square.

"You went down it," Pyke says, stopping his coiling. "Two hundred, you say. Under my ground. I chained the top two summers ago. Six of them stood there with a theodolite, and I took them for a road party." He shakes his head. "Two hundred men. There aren't two hundred men in Rivermark."

choices.label: There is now. They're just not above ground.

greeting.text: "You got as far as the stair and came back up," Pyke says. He doesn't think less of you; he's spent forty-three years avoiding holes himself. "Sensible. There's nothing at the bottom of a hole that needs finding by anyone who isn't paid to find it." He coils the chain. "That's the most useful thing my father ever told me. I've never tested it."

choices.label: Somebody's paying two hundred men to find it.
I've seen your mark in two places now.

greeting.text: "Down at the head of the valley," Pyke says when you mention it. He nods and keeps coiling. "That's the works. I chained the ground over it two summers ago. Took a week. I've never been down, and I don't want to. I'm sixty-one and I like a sky."

choices.label: I've seen your mark in two places now.

greeting.text: An old man sits on the granary steps, a hundred feet of chain over one shoulder and bread in a cloth. He nods, sizing you up as possible work. "Chainman," he says around a mouthful. "Pyke. If you want a boundary walked, it's a shilling, and I'll want a boy."

choices.label: I've seen your mark in two places now.

what_a_chainman_does.text: "Drags a chain," Pyke says. "A hundred feet makes a chain. Somebody sights a line; I walk it and call the count. Somebody writes it down. Then I paint a mark at the end so the next man knows where I stopped." He finishes his bread. "Forty-three years. My father did it too. It's not interesting, and I'm not going to pretend it is."

choices.label: Who wants lines walked in Rivermark?

the_mark.text: He holds the bob still so you can see its flat face. "That's a survey mark," he says. "Bob in a square. Means a line was measured from here, and the measurement's good." He lets it swing again. "I paint about forty a season. There's one on the granary corner behind you, if you look. I put it there in spring. Nobody's looked at it since, me included."

interjections.text: Sera goes still. "Forty a season," she says. "For how many seasons?"
Ilse: "There's one cut into stone forty feet under the warren. Did you paint that one?" Pyke, at ease: "Not me. I don't go down holes."

choices.label: Who tells you where to walk?
I'm going to start writing down where I see it.
Then it's a maker's mark and I'm wasting your afternoon.

he_does_not_know.text: "A boy brings me a paper on Monday with the lines on it," Pyke says. "I walk them, then hand the count in at the counting house on Friday. That's where I'm paid, too." He shrugs. "I've never asked. In forty-three years, nobody's told a chainman anything, and no chainman has wanted to know. You'd be surprised how restful it is."

choices.label: No. I don't think I would be.

it_does_not.text: "I'm sixty-one," Pyke says, "and I'm paid in coin on the day by people who've never argued over a count. Do you know how rare that is? Marrow argues. The council argues. The priory spent two years arguing over a hedge." He picks up the chain. "Whoever they are, they pay on the day. That's all I've ever needed to know."

choices.label: One day it might not be.

he_gives_you_the_bob.text: Pyke laughs as if you've made his week. Then he pulls a spare bob from his coat and puts it in your hand. "There. Now you've got the mark, and I don't have to lend you mine every time you want to compare one." He's still smiling when you leave. He goes on painting them.

no_harm_done.text: "No harm in it," Pyke says. "Everybody notices the marks eventually. Nobody's ever come back twice." He shoulders the chain and heads up the lane to walk someone's line. You stand there a moment with the answer you'd asked for.

whose_wages.text: "Counting house," he says. "Friday. One and threepence a day, with the boy's tuppence coming out of that." You wait for more. He looks puzzled. "That's it. The whole of it. I'm not on anybody's household. I'd have to eat at their table, and I'd rather not."

choices.label: The counting house doesn't pay you. It honours a note. Whose?

the_tray.text: "Under the long desk," Pyke says. "They keep each honoured note for a year, then burn it. Nobody minds you looking. There's nothing in them, just a receipt for a chainman's fortnight." He returns to the chain. "You'll want the one with my name spelt wrong. They all spell it wrong."

read_the_note.text: Pyke turns it over and reads it properly this time. His face changes, and doesn't quite settle back. "Huh," he says. "No. There's initials, and there's the bob-and-square. That's not... A house signs. A house always signs." He hands it back. "I've had a hundred of these. Never once turned one over."

interjections.text: Sera: "The counting house honours an unsigned note because they know the mark. They've seen it often enough to recognise it."
Aldric: "Forty-three years, and the first time you look at the back of one, there's no name."

choices.label: Ask the counting house whose mark it is.
Put it back in the tray.

the_name.text: The clerk doesn't need to look it up. "Corse," he says, like a word he's written four hundred times without saying aloud. "Ludo Corse, factor, at Greyhythe. It's a good mark. We honour it same-day." He returns to his work. Outside, Pyke drags the chain up the lane, calling the count to nobody.

interjections.text: Kessa: "Have you heard of him?" The clerk doesn't look up. "No. Why would I? He pays."

put_it_back.text: You return the note to the tray. In eleven months, a clerk will burn it with four hundred others. Pyke will be paid on Friday. That will be that.

the_address.text: "Down the river stair, then eleven miles along the towpath," Pyke says. "Greyhythe. Ask for the factor's house. There's only one, above the new landing." He thinks a moment. "Take him something. He won't want it, but he'll be pleased you thought of it. That's the only advice I've got. I've had three years to come up with better."

how_many.text: Pyke works it out there on the spot. "Forty a season. Three years." His lips move. "Call it three hundred and some." He looks up the lane at the mark he painted on the granary corner in spring. "That's a lot of line for a valley this size. I'll grant you that."

of_course_i_knew.text: "Ground somebody's buying," Pyke says. It's the ordinary answer, and he's given it before. "You measure what you're buying, then measure it again before you pay. That's all a survey is: a man making sure he isn't cheated." He coils the chain. "They've measured this valley as thoroughly as I've ever measured anything."

that_is_him.text: "That's him," Pyke says. "He'll answer anything. My boy once asked what he did. Corse sat on a crate and told him for a quarter of an hour. The boy came away none the wiser and very pleased." He winds the chain. "I've thought about that since. Couldn't tell you why."

choices.label: How many marks have you painted for him?

he_reads_it.text: He reads it aloud in the lane, standing in the rain. He can read a survey and you can't. Weirs. Seams. Roofs. At sheet six, he stops, goes back a line, and reads it again. Then he says, steady as ever, "That's not how you enter a town. You enter a town as a place. That's entered as a cost." After a while, he adds, "Under clearance."

interjections.text: Aldric takes off his hat. You've only seen him do that at gravesides.
Ilse: "Say the figure." Pyke does. Nobody speaks for a while.
Kessa: "Who do we hit?" Pyke keeps looking at the sheet. "Nobody. That's the trouble with it. There's nobody in it at all."

the_reading.text: It takes an hour. People stop at the shouting on the granary steps, then stay to hear what Pyke is saying. Reed comes to listen and write. Marrow's people come out onto the weighing floor and stand there. At the end, a woman asks what the town should do. Pyke says he doesn't know; he's a chainman. He climbs down and coils his chain. His employment in the valley is over.

the_burning.text: He doesn't argue. He holds the sheets while you light the tinder, which you hadn't expected. In the rain, he watches nine sheets, three years, and about four hundred days of somebody's wages burn. "They'll do it again," he says. "They'll want a chainman." He pauses. "I'll take the work. I want you to know now, so you don't hear it from someone else later."

he_lets_you_keep_it.text: "Right," Pyke says. He helps you roll it, ties it, then hands it back. "Then you've got a thing that eleven hundred people are in, and none of them know it." He shoulders the chain. "Mind how you carry that. Paper's the only part of this anybody's ever taken seriously."

no_such_thing.text: "There isn't a right thing," Pyke says. "There's a chain, a line, and a count. After that, it's somebody else's arithmetic." He looks at the coil in his lap. "For forty-three years I've been the man who doesn't ask. Turns out that was a job too, and I was good at it."

they_are_asking.text: "A man came up from downriver asking who was at the works that week," Pyke says. "Polite. Bought me a drink. Wrote down what I told him, which was nothing, then thanked me and paid for the drink." He draws the chain straight. "He'll be back. That sort always comes back on a Tuesday."
